meta.title: Autumn Budget 2026
meta.statusNote: Healey is on his feet in the Commons. Announcements are added here as he makes them. Badenoch replies afterwards, and the OBR press conference is at 14:30.

measures.headline: £100 Household Energy Payment this winter
measures.detail: About 20 million households in council tax bands A to D will get £100 paid straight into their bank accounts this winter. It costs £2.6bn. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland get funding and are being urged to pass it on.
measures.impact: If your home is in council tax band A, B, C or D in England, expect £100 towards energy bills over winter. Elsewhere in the UK, it depends on your devolved government.

measures.headline: Standing charges on gas bills scrapped
measures.detail: Confirmed in the speech: Ofgem will remove the fixed daily standing charge from household gas bills from next year. Similar reforms are planned for electricity.
measures.impact: The charge is about £108 a year now, but the cost is expected to move into the price per unit of gas. Martin Lewis estimates around 60% of households will pay less, mostly low users, and 40% will pay more. Reports put typical savings at roughly £22 to £50 a year.

measures.headline: Cash ISA limit stays at £20,000
measures.detail: The previous plan to cut the cash ISA allowance from £20,000 to £12,000 for under-65s, due from April 2027, has been dropped. So has a plan to tax cash held inside Stocks and Shares ISAs.
measures.impact: Nothing changes. You can still put up to £20,000 a year into ISAs tax-free, all in cash if you like.

measures.headline: No rise in income tax, employee NI or VAT rates
measures.detail: The Chancellor has ruled out raising the rates of income tax, employee National Insurance and VAT, sticking to Labour's 2024 manifesto promise.
measures.impact: The rates on your payslip and on most shopping won't go up. Taxes can still rise in other ways, though, for example by keeping thresholds frozen.

measures.headline: Will the tax-free allowance finally rise?
measures.detail: The £12,570 personal allowance has been frozen since April 2021. A higher allowance has been floated as a key promise, but no figure or funding has been confirmed.
measures.impact: If it rises, everyone earning over £12,570 would take home a little more. If it stays frozen, more of your pay rise gets taxed (this is called fiscal drag).

measures.headline: VAT cut on electricity extended to July
measures.detail: The existing VAT cut on household electricity, covering 29 million households, is extended through winter and spring until July.
measures.impact: Worth about £50 off the annual energy price cap for a typical household.

measures.headline: Higher tax-free mileage rate
measures.detail: The tax-free rate for using your own car for work becomes a permanent 55p a mile for the first 10,000 miles. Beyond that it goes up from 25p to 35p a mile.
measures.impact: If you drive your own car for work, you can be paid more per mile without paying tax on it.

measures.headline: Import tariffs scrapped on 100+ supermarket items
measures.detail: Tariffs are being removed on more than 100 everyday products sold in supermarkets.
measures.impact: Estimated to save the average family about £21 a year on food shopping, if shops pass it on.

measures.headline: Paternity pay for the self-employed
measures.detail: Self-employed new parents can get up to two weeks of statutory paternity pay, worth up to £194 a week.
measures.impact: Self-employed dads and partners can take time off after a birth without losing all their income.

measures.headline: No income tax on a full State Pension
measures.detail: A new Pension Tax Allowance means pensioners whose income is no more than the full new State Pension won't pay income tax for the rest of this Parliament. Separately, ex-miners get every penny of their pension fund surplus.
measures.impact: Pensioners living on just the State Pension won't be dragged into income tax as the pension rises.

measures.headline: Minimum wage up 3.9%
measures.detail: Both the National Minimum Wage and the National Living Wage rise by 3.9%, covering 2.3 million of the lowest-paid workers.
measures.impact: A pay rise for the lowest-paid, normally from April. For a full-time worker it's roughly in line with inflation.

measures.headline: Carer's Allowance 'cliff edge' replaced with a taper
measures.detail: Instead of losing all of Carer's Allowance for earning £1 over the weekly limit, carers will lose £1 of support for every £1 they earn above it.
measures.impact: Carers can take on a few extra hours of paid work without suddenly losing the whole allowance. But the Lib Dems say it won't start for four years, and losing £1 for every £1 earned is effectively a 100% tax on those extra earnings.

measures.headline: Extra £432m to tackle rough sleeping
measures.detail: Funding for rough sleeping support is expected to double, including £432m aimed at getting people off the streets before Christmas.
measures.impact: More emergency accommodation and support services this winter.

measures.headline: 5p fuel duty cut extended to July
measures.detail: The 5p cut in fuel duty, and the low rate on red diesel, are extended through winter and spring until July.
measures.impact: No rise at the pump from duty for now. That helps drivers, hauliers and farmers. The question returns next summer.

measures.headline: More energy help for lower-income homes
measures.detail: An expansion of the Warm Homes scheme is expected, which helps lower-income households with energy costs and insulation. It could be paid for by the bank levy.
measures.impact: If you're on a lower income, you could get more help with bills or home upgrades this winter. Details to come.

measures.headline: 25% off electricity bills for 10,000 firms
measures.detail: The British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme will cut electricity bills by 25% for around 10,000 businesses from April, with backdated payments for this year's energy costs.
measures.impact: Big help for energy-heavy manufacturers. Most small businesses won't qualify.

measures.headline: Temporary rise in the bank tax surcharge
measures.detail: Banks pay a 3% surcharge on profits on top of 25% corporation tax. Healey is reported to be raising it temporarily, but to below the 8% it stood at until 2023.
measures.impact: Raises money from big banks' profits rather than households directly. Banks could pass some of the cost on through savings and loan rates. Bank shares rose on the news because the rise is smaller than feared.

measures.headline: 70,000 more small firms pay no business rates
measures.detail: For retail, hospitality and leisure businesses, the Small Business Rate Relief threshold rises from £12,000 to £18,000.
measures.impact: 70,000 more shops, cafés, pubs and gyms pay no business rates at all. Half of all shops, restaurants and gyms will now pay none.

measures.headline: £10m duty relief for small brewers and cider makers
measures.detail: About 2,000 small British brewers and cider makers get £10m of alcohol duty relief.
measures.impact: Helps small independent producers, and may soften the effect of the general alcohol duty rise.

measures.headline: Alcohol duty to rise with inflation (about 2p a pint)
measures.detail: Reports suggest alcohol duty will go up in line with RPI inflation (3.9%), which works out at about 2p on a pint of beer.
measures.impact: A small rise at the bar and in shops. Pubs say it adds to their costs. Not confirmed yet.

measures.headline: Tax on rental profits could rise by 2 points
measures.detail: Pre-Budget reporting suggests a 2 percentage point rise in the tax on rental income from 2027/28.
measures.impact: Landlords would pay more tax on rental profits. Some of the cost could be passed on to tenants. Not confirmed yet.

updates.title: £10m relief for small brewers
updates.body: About 2,000 small brewers and cider makers get £10m in alcohol duty relief.

updates.title: Business rates scrapped for 70,000 more small firms
updates.body: The small business rates relief threshold for shops, hospitality and leisure rises from £12,000 to £18,000. Half of shops, restaurants and gyms will now pay no business rates.

updates.title: Paid paternity leave for the self-employed
updates.body: For the first time, self-employed fathers and partners will be eligible for paid parental leave. Healey calls it a 'downpayment'.

updates.title: Minimum wage up 3.9%
updates.body: The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage both rise by 3.9%, covering 2.3 million low-paid workers.

updates.title: No income tax for pensioners on the State Pension
updates.body: A new Pension Tax Allowance means pensioners with income up to the full new State Pension won't pay income tax this Parliament. Ex-miners get the full pension fund surplus.

updates.title: Fuel duty cut extended to July
updates.body: The 5p fuel duty cut and the low red diesel rate are extended to July because of high fuel prices. The higher mileage rate goes from 25p to 35p a mile.

updates.title: Tariffs suspended on 100+ supermarket items
updates.body: Confirmed in the speech, to help keep the weekly shop down.

updates.title: £100 energy payment for 20 million homes
updates.body: Households in council tax bands A–D get £100 paid directly into their bank accounts this winter to help with energy bills, at a cost of £2.6bn.

updates.title: Confirmed: gas standing charges scrapped
updates.body: Healey confirmed Ofgem will remove gas standing charges, which cost over £100 a year whatever you use, from next year. Electricity is to follow.

updates.title: Electricity VAT cut extended, worth £50
updates.body: The VAT cut on electricity is extended through winter and spring to July, taking about £50 off the annual price cap. Around 10,000 businesses get 25% off electricity from April.

updates.title: Energy shake-up to cut bills
updates.body: New clean power projects will only go ahead if they lower bills. More existing renewables move onto fixed-price contracts to shield bills from gas prices, and grid connections get faster through GB Grid.

updates.title: Cheaper energy is 'top priority'
updates.body: Healey says cheaper energy is the government's top priority, with clean power central to it. Net Zero by 2050 stays.

updates.title: 'Radical reform' of energy promised
updates.body: Healey points to approval of the Jackdaw gas field, which protects hundreds of jobs and is worth an estimated £2.9bn, and a new Energy Wealth Fund for the UK.

updates.title: Growth forecast upgraded
updates.body: The OBR now expects growth of 1.2% this year and 1% next year, then 1.6% in 2028, 1.8% in 2029, 1.7% in 2030 and 1.6% in 2031.

updates.title: Swipe at Liz Truss
updates.body: Healey said the last time the IMF singled out the UK was when Truss 'crashed the economy'. This time, he said, the IMF projects the UK's deficit will be the lowest in the G7 by 2029.

updates.title: OBR forecasts: borrowing falling, debt flat
updates.body: Borrowing is forecast at 4.2% of GDP this year, falling to 3.4% next year, 2.1% in 2029/30 and 1.8% by 2031/32. Debt hovers around 83–84% of GDP before easing to 81.7% by 2031/32.

updates.title: Headroom of £15bn, and no 'broad-based' tax rises
updates.body: Healey ruled out broad tax rises and deep cuts to public services. The OBR puts his buffer against the fiscal rules at £15bn in 2029/30, rising to £22bn in 2030/31. He says the day-to-day deficit will be gone within three years.

updates.title: Rowdy Commons
updates.body: Deputy Speaker Nusrat Ghani called for order twice in seven minutes as opposition MPs jeered.

updates.title: Middle East war has pushed inflation back up
updates.body: The OBR says the Middle East conflict is a key driver of its forecasts. Oil has gone from about $70 to well over $100 a barrel, and gas prices have nearly tripled since February. Inflation, which was due to fall to 2% this year, has risen again as a result.

updates.title: 'Fiscal discipline is my first commitment'
updates.body: Healey says the Budget meets both fiscal rules: day-to-day spending is covered by taxes, and debt falls as a share of the economy. He wants to keep cutting borrowing so less goes on debt interest.

updates.title: Tribute to Reeves, and a Gogglebox joke
updates.body: Healey praised Rachel Reeves, Britain's first female Chancellor, for fiscal discipline and cutting NHS waiting lists. He joked that he'd hoped to be the most-watched minister this week, until the PM turned up on Gogglebox.

updates.title: Three priorities: costs, business, and public services
updates.body: Healey's priorities are 'breathing space' on household and business costs, backing British firms to grow, and action on energy, national security, public services and housing. He says the Budget offers 'fresh hope' and ties it to a 10-Year Plan and next year's Spending Review.

updates.title: 'A Budget for the working people of Britain'
updates.body: Healey opens by calling this a Budget for working people and businesses of all sizes, built on fiscal discipline.

updates.title: Healey is on his feet
updates.body: The Chancellor has stood up at the dispatch box to begin his first Budget speech.

updates.title: Borrowing is running above forecast
updates.body: The government borrowed £24.5bn last month, more than expected. That takes borrowing so far this financial year to £97.8bn, about £6bn above the OBR's forecast, which leaves Healey little room for giveaways.

updates.title: Lib Dems: carers' fix is too slow and too harsh
updates.body: Ed Davey welcomed the end of the Carer's Allowance cliff edge but said it won't take effect for four years. Taking back £1 for every £1 earned amounts to a '100% tax rate' for working carers, he said.

updates.title: PMQs underway before the Budget
updates.body: Andy Burnham opened Prime Minister's Questions at 12:04. Kemi Badenoch pressed him on the EU, and Burnham said there's 'no confusion': Labour's red lines, including no return to free movement, stay for this Parliament. The Budget speech follows straight after.

updates.title: Energy help could be funded by the banks
updates.body: Healey has promised 'breathing space' on costs. More support for lower-income homes through the Warm Homes scheme is tipped, possibly paid for by the bank levy. Tax changes are also expected.

updates.title: Red box out on the steps of No 11
updates.body: Healey posed with the red Budget box outside Downing Street and is heading to the Commons for his first Budget speech.

updates.title: Five 'everyday fixes' already announced
updates.body: Ahead of the speech, the government confirmed: a taper replacing the Carer's Allowance cliff edge, tariffs dropped on 100+ supermarket items (about £21 a year per family), higher tax-free mileage rates, paternity pay for the self-employed (up to £194 a week for two weeks), and 1,000 Post Office drop boxes. Healey admits they 'are not going to change the world'.

updates.title: Bank tax to rise, but temporarily
updates.body: Bloomberg reports Healey will temporarily raise the bank surcharge from its current 3%, but keep it below 8%. Lloyds, Barclays and NatWest shares rose at least 2% on relief that it isn't higher.

updates.title: Drivers watch fuel duty
updates.body: The 5p fuel duty cut is due to start ending in January. Healey wouldn't say beforehand whether he'll delay the rise, and motoring groups are pushing for a further cut.

updates.title: Fewer firms are exporting
updates.body: Among businesses turning over at least £500,000, the share that have ever exported fell from 45% in 2021 to 35% in 2025, according to a government survey. Expect growth and trade to feature in the speech.

updates.title: Who is John Healey?
updates.body: Healey, Labour MP for Rawmarsh and Conisbrough, became Chancellor on 20 July 2026, taking over from Rachel Reeves. Today is his first Budget in the job.

updates.title: The debt backdrop
updates.body: With national debt around £3 trillion, the UK now spends more on debt interest than on defence, schools and prisons combined. Commentators want to see how Healey funds NATO targets of 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

updates.title: Today's timetable, and more expected measures
updates.body: After PMQs, Healey speaks at 12:30. Kemi Badenoch replies for the Conservatives at around 13:30, and the OBR gives its press conference on the forecasts at 14:30. Also tipped: a minimum wage rise, an end to the carers' earnings 'cliff edge', and £432m for rough sleeping.

updates.title: What's already ruled out, and what to watch for
updates.body: Healey has ruled out higher rates of income tax, employee National Insurance and VAT. The big questions for 12:30 are whether the £12,570 tax-free allowance, frozen since 2021, finally goes up, and whether VAT comes off electricity bills.

updates.title: Martin Lewis: most will pay less, but not everyone
updates.body: The money expert welcomed scrapping the gas standing charge, currently about £108 a year. He estimates around 60% of households will pay less and 40% more, as the cost moves into the price per unit. He also warned that the January price cap could rise by around 27%.

updates.title: Alcohol duty expected to rise with inflation
updates.body: Reports say alcohol duty will go up in line with RPI inflation (3.9%), adding about 2p to a pint. Pub groups warn this adds pressure on struggling venues.

updates.title: Business owners call for 'courage'
updates.body: A London bakery founder says rising minimum wage costs are putting firms off taking on trainees and apprentices, and wants the Chancellor to be bolder.

updates.title: Greens: scrapping standing charges is 'tinkering'
updates.body: The Green Party says the gas standing charge move doesn't go far enough on the cost of living.

updates.title: Fuel poverty campaigners welcome the move, with caveats
updates.body: The End Fuel Poverty Coalition calls it 'real relief' for many households but warns that some won't see savings.

updates.title: Gas standing charges to be scrapped
updates.body: The Treasury confirms standing charges on household gas bills will be removed from 2027, or as soon as possible after.

updates.title: Cash ISA cut dropped
updates.body: John Healey has scrapped Rachel Reeves's plan to cut the cash ISA limit to £12,000 for under-65s. The limit stays at £20,000.

updates.title: Expect a cautious Budget
updates.body: Room for manoeuvre is tight because of high debt costs and talk of a possible December election. Most commentators expect few big surprises.

updates.title: It's Budget Day
updates.body: The Chancellor's first priority is expected to be reassuring bond markets. The speech is due around 12:30.
